The lighthouse on the point has stood since 1874. Its keeper climbs one hundred and twelve stone steps to reach the lamp room, where a Fresnel lens bends the light of a single flame into a beam seen twenty miles out to sea.

Sourdough rises without any yeast from a packet. A starter of flour and water, fed every day, keeps wild yeasts and lactic acid bacteria alive; mixed into the dough, they give off carbon dioxide, which the gluten traps in small pockets, and the loaf swells over several hours before it is baked.

An octopus can change the colour and texture of its skin in a fraction of a second. Thousands of chromatophores, small sacs of pigment ringed by muscle, open and close under the control of its nerves, and raised papillae let it mimic the bumps of a rock or the fronds of seaweed.

A glacier flows downhill under its own weight. The ice deforms slowly, like very stiff putty, and where meltwater reaches the bed the whole mass can slide; most valley glaciers move a few tens of centimetres a day, though some outlet glaciers in Greenland travel more than forty metres.

The first moves of a chess game are about the centre and development. Players bring their knights and bishops out early, contest the four central squares, and castle to tuck the king behind a wall of pawns before the middle game begins.

On a bicycle, a small chainring at the front and a large sprocket at the back give a low gear. Each turn of the pedals moves the bike a shorter distance, so climbing a steep hill takes less force, at the price of pedalling faster for the same speed.

A honeybee colony is a single household of tens of thousands of insects, and almost all of them are female. The queen is the mother of the colony: in the height of summer she may lay more than a thousand eggs a day, one in each cell the workers have cleaned and polished for her, and the scent she gives off tells the whole hive that she is alive and laying. She does not rule in any sense a person would recognise. The workers decide where to forage, when to build new comb, when to raise new queens and when to swarm, and they make those decisions collectively, through dances, through the exchange of food from mouth to mouth, and through the chemical signals that pass among them in the dark of the hive. A worker's life follows her age. In her first days she cleans cells; then she feeds the larvae on brood food made in glands in her head; then she builds comb from wax she secretes from glands on the underside of her abdomen; then she guards the entrance, sniffing every bee that lands to be sure it belongs. Only in the last two or three weeks of her life does she leave to forage, flying up to several kilometres from the hive for nectar, pollen, water and the resin the colony uses to seal gaps. A forager that finds a rich patch of flowers returns and dances on the comb: the angle of her waggle run against the vertical gives the direction of the flowers against the sun, and the length of the run gives the distance. Her sisters follow her through the dance, taste the nectar she brings, and fly out to find the place for themselves. Nectar is carried home in the honey stomach, passed from bee to bee, and spread thin in open cells, where the workers fan their wings until enough water has evaporated; then they cap the cell with wax, and the honey keeps for years. Drones, the males, are raised in larger cells in spring and summer. They do no work in the hive and have no sting; their one purpose is to mate with a queen from another colony, high in the air at a gathering place they find by some means not fully understood, and they die in the act. In autumn the workers stop feeding the drones that remain and drag them out of the entrance. Through the winter the colony survives on its stored honey, clustered in a ball around the queen, the bees on the inside shivering their flight muscles to make heat and the bees on the outside packed close to hold it in, changing places through the long cold months so that none freezes. When spring comes and the first willow and crocus flower, the queen begins to lay again, the cluster loosens, and the year starts over. A colony that grows crowded in late spring raises new queens and swarms: the old queen leaves with about half the workers, who gorge on honey before they go, and the swarm hangs from a branch while scouts search for a hollow tree or an empty box. Each scout that finds a likely cavity dances for it, more vigorously the better it judges the site, and other scouts go to inspect it; over a day or two the support for one site grows until the scouts at it reach a quorum, and then the whole swarm takes to the air and flies there together, guided by the few who know the way.
